walkthrough_label: Example Patient B - abnormal S1 (the 'elective' patient who isn't well today)
reason_answer: To have my gallbladder taken out.

presentation.summary: Mrs Ahmed, 61, is booked for planned keyhole gallbladder removal. Her daughter noticed yellow eyes last week and she has dark urine: a stone may have moved into the main bile duct.

history.answer: Some aching under the ribs on and off.
My daughter said my eyes looked a bit yellow last week. And my urine has been dark like tea. No fever or shivering.
Gallstones, found on a scan last year.
No anaesthetic problems in the family.
Tea and a biscuit yesterday evening at 20:00, nothing since.

observations.note: No fever: probably no infection in the duct (yet).

examination.finding: Yellow tinge to the whites of the eyes.
Mild tenderness under the right ribs; no guarding; no lump.
Skin is not itchy-scratched; no rash.

results.comment: About 3 times normal: bile duct cells irritated by blockage
Confirms the ALP is coming from the bile system
Moderately raised: liver cells irritated by backed-up bile
Normal: no strong sign of infection
Clotting normal (a long blockage could raise it)

scores.name: Bile-duct-stone risk
scores.note: Bilirubin above 68 micromol/L plus a duct wider than 6 mm (ASGE 2019)

problems.label: Probable stone in the main bile duct: not what she was booked for
problems.why: Jaundice, cholestatic liver tests and a 9 mm duct make a duct stone likely; operating on the gallbladder alone would leave it in place.
expected_actions: Ask the red-flag questions and look at her eyes
Request liver tests and an ultrasound
Do not proceed today; call the senior surgeon

problems.label: Watch for infection of the duct (cholangitis)
problems.why: No fever, shivering or low BP today, but it can develop.
expected_actions: Check temperature, pulse and BP again
Give her safety-net advice: fever, shivering or worse pain means come straight back

decisions.prompt: Bilirubin 72 and the bile duct is 9 mm on ultrasound. What now?

options.text: High risk of a duct stone: do not proceed today, call the senior surgeon, plan ERCP before the gallbladder operation

options.consequence: The stone would stay in the duct: risk of cholangitis or pancreatitis.

options.text: Proceed and order an MRCP afterwards
options.consequence: MRCP is for intermediate risk before the operation; this is high risk.

decisions.prompt: Is there any sign of cholangitis today (fever, shivering, low BP)?

options.text: No: she has no fever, normal BP and pulse
options.consequence: Not the emergency branch; the high-risk pathway applies.

decisions.prompt: What safety-net advice do you give Mrs Ahmed?

options.text: If you get a fever, shivering or worse pain, come straight back: it could be an infection in the duct

options.consequence: The risk of infection remains until the stone is cleared.

correct: Ask the red-flag questions: yellow eyes, dark urine, fever, pain
Stop today's plan; senior; ERCP pathway
Explain to Mrs Ahmed, document, safety-net advice

incorrect.mistake: Ignores the abnormal liver tests and goes ahead
incorrect.shows: The senior or anaesthetist character stops the case
incorrect.recovery: Review the results and call the senior

missed: Does not ask about yellow eyes or look: the liver tests (if ordered) still flag it
recovery: Recognise from the tests, then call the senior

recognised: Jaundice picked up from the history and examination
debrief.priority: A probable duct stone in a planned patient
debrief.related: Jaundice, cholestatic tests and the wide duct all come from the same blocked duct
debrief.trigger_escalation: Yellow eyes, dark urine, abnormal liver tests
debrief.if_ignored: A stone left in the duct can cause life-threatening infection
debrief.remember: Ask about yellow eyes in every gallstone patient

asa.why: A stone that may have moved into the bile duct, with jaundice: a mild to severe systemic problem (ASA 2 to 3).
